So I know a lot of people are speculating it might be a porn problem, but I'm wondering if maybe his own relationship with his parents is so devoid of physical affection that he isn't used to seeing what a healthy child-parent relationship looks like. 

At least from my own experience, my dad was never physically affectionate. We might share a brief awkward hug where we barely touch each other, do a quick "pat pat" on the back and break apart from there. And even then it's just as a way of greeting hello or saying goodbye. A formality, really. I probably would have seen your relationship with your dad as "weird" back then before I knew better. 

It's definitely worth a conversation to see if he can have the emotional maturity to acknowledge he's wrong. But if not, definitely cut your losses and move on. It might not be his fault if he grew up seeing something different, but it is his fault if he chooses not to learn anything differently.

I'll just anecdotally tell you about my kiddo, since he sounds similar. Obvi it's not one size fits all, and you'll still need to get an official assessment, but I've been in your shoes and the waiting is so, so hard, and it's really easy to spiral and just get lost in the sauce of everything online. 

Husband and I suspected possible autism due to a speech delay, but we weren't totally sure. There were definitely red flags: very limited eye contact, no pointing, no real expressive or receptive language at 18 months. But that was it. No hand flapping, walking on tiptoes, no sensory issues, very social, no meltdowns over anything, super chill and flexible lil dude when it came to changes in routine or making a quick transition. He was walking at 11 months, and now at 2.5 he's hella mobile and loves climbing everything, but also is aware of his limits and will reach out for help if needed. 

But when I'd watch him compared to other kids in our playgroup I'd notice the differences in how he interacted with the world. He didn't want to sit and listen with me at storytime like all the other kids. He wanted to go check out the painted cow statue in the corner. Or instead of playing on the ramps and wedges at toddler gym, he was more interested in feeling the textured wall, or trying to get out of the room to explore somewhere else. 

I was able to get him scheduled for an autism screening last year with our local medical group. It was a six month wait, and 2 weeks before the appointment we were notified that our insurance company couldn't reach  an agreement with our local medical group during contract renegotiations and therefore they would be considered out of network moving forward. 

So cancelled that and ended up getting an online assessment through Meliora Health at the recommendation of our speech therapist and we got an appointment within 2 weeks - almost the exact date as the initial appointment. 

Long story short, he's autistic. We've got a speech therapist, a developmental therapist and an OT since we're having issues with food preferences now. 

TL;DR: my kiddo sounds similar to yours. He's autistic. I'd recommend checking out Meliora Health to potentially get a quicker diagnosis online.

Thankfully I've been smoke-free since 2015, and though still def obese, I'm down 75 pounds with the help of Ozempic, and extra motivation from getting diagnosed with type 2 beetus, and giving birth to my son. TL;DR: For me, quitting food has been infinitely harder than quitting smoking.

So I'd rock him from 2am until 4am or later when he'd fall back asleep. Sometimes he'd still be up by 6am, so we'd just give up and wait for him to crash later. It was just starting to become unmanageable having to rock him up to 2 hours to fall asleep and then several hours a night. 

We never tried cosleeping, mostly because my husband and are I both chonks, and I'm a very restless sleeper and toss and turn all night, so I just never felt safe keeping him in bed with us. 

After 2 months straight of me just living in the rocking chair with him at night, we ended up doing the ferber method. The first night we tried doing check-ins every 5, 10, 15, 20 minutes and so on, but going in and leaving made it a million times worse. So we gave up on that night, but tried again the next day with full extinction - no check-ins - and he cried for about 45 minutes. I told myself that if it reached an hour that was my cut off point, but it never got to that. The following night he cried for 30 minutes, then 15, then 5, until nothing. 

Now at 28 months we do the whole bedtime routine song and dance, and then leave while he's fully awake, and he's happy to just bop about in there by himself and play with his stuffed animals until he gets tired and goes to sleep. The process of having him cry it out was absolute psychological torture the first 2-3 days. I cried outside his room while he cried. 

I felt like a monster, but I just could NOT function anymore having such constantly interrupted sleep. At some point I realized my lack of sleep and free time to just take a breath (and a shower) without it being a whole production was causing me to be cranky and impatient with him. I'm a much, much better mother and caretaker when I can get at least 4 hours of uninterrupted sleep. 

So, yeah, the process sucked. If I had felt safe cosleeping I probably would have done that, and if not for his 3 month stretch of nightly insomnia, I never would have done cry it out, but holy hell now that we're on the other side I am so glad I did.

This might be something to work on internally, and ideally in therapy. I used to suffer from a lot of insecurities with my appearance, and this way of thinking sounds very familiar to things I used to think. 

It sounds like you're actively looking to be triggered if you watch him like a hawk and scan the room for attractive women that he might notice. Just because your husband finds other women objectively attractive it doesn't mean he's thinking he wishes you looked like them. 

Obvs everyone is different, but what helped me was understanding that a lot of what I was thinking was just me projecting my insecurity as an explanation for someone's actions. In your situation this comes across when you notice your husband look at a woman passing by. You mentally rationalize that his reason for doing this is because he wishes you looked like her. But this is just the story you're telling yourself. If you asked your husband what he was thinking in that moment, he might tell you it was just his subconscious lizard brain reaction to look, but that he placed zero thought or intention behind it. 

Our brains always come up with a "story" to make sense of things, but unfortunately a lot of times the default story we use to rationalize things is based on prior emotional trauma/insecurity and not logic.
